Paradox: P(A|B) is not the same as P(B|A)



This, as we can see, an imperfect but reasonably good test.
There’s a problem, though. Can anybody spot it?
If we already know somebody’s HIV status, why would be bother
giving them a test? Far, far more often, when we think about the
accuracy of a test, we are actually interested in the reverse
question:
Sensitivity and Specificity describe a situation where we already
know somebody’s HIV status. Why test if we already know? What we usually
really want a different thing

-Think about that. If you pick a person at random, give them an HIV
test and it comes back positive, there is a 3% chance that they actually
have HIV. 97% of them are getting a positive test (and, likely, quite a
scare) erroneously.

This goes against most people’s expectations. Why this happens
actually isn’t that hard to understand. Of people with HIV, 99% will get
a positive test result.
Of people who don’t have HIV, only 3% will get a positive test
result.
But, the important fact is that HIV is actually quite rare. 3% of
a big population is bigger than 99% of a very small population.
So, this test is 99% accurate at detecting HIV among people who
have it, but for a random person getting a test, a positive test result
is only accurate 3.4% percent of the time.
My point here is not that these tests are worthless. Rather what
I want to point out is that probability is often unpredictable and
unintuitive.

Bayesian Updating: What it is not

Statistical Rethinking, p.2 (Richard McElreath, 2020)

Bayesian Updating: What it is
Instead of tests, we have Bayesian Updating:

We have a prior belief about the world (specifically, about a parameter or “estimand”).I think that about 60% of Kathmandu will vote for the current mayor in the next election.
Then, we observe something, and we estimate the likelihood of what we saw.I just took a survey, and only 30% of people said they will vote for the current mayor. This doesn’t really fit with what I expected.
This new observation changes our prior belief (challenging it or making it stronger), to become our posterior.I now think that about 45% of Kathmandu will vote for the current mayor in the next election.


So I said that we were going to derive our entire statistics from
first principles, and I meant it. Instead of a million pre-built tests,
we have one process: Bayesian updating
A million tests. We have one process, called Bayesian updating.
Everything we build will be an application of that same logic.

library(knitr)

library(tidyverse)

library(cmdstanr)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

filename <- "../datasets/wb2022.csv"
filename2 <- "../datasets/wb_country.csv"

# build a variable label vector for better labelling of df
label_vec <- read_csv(filename) |>
  distinct(`Series Code`, `Series Name`) |>
  filter(!is.na(`Series Code`), !is.na(`Series Name`)) |>
  group_by(`Series Code`) |> # in case of duplicates
  summarise(label = first(`Series Name`), .groups = "drop") |>
  with(setNames(label, `Series Code`))

# compose dataframe
df <- read_csv(filename) |>
  select(-c(`Series Name`)) |>
  slice(1:(n() - 5)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("^\\d{4} \\[YR\\d{4}\\]$"),
    names_to = "year",
    values_to = "value",
    names_transform = list(year = ~ str_extract(.x, "^\\d{4}"))
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = `Series Code`, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(across(
    any_of(names(label_vec)),
    ~ {
      attr(.x, "label") <- unname(label_vec[cur_column()])
      .x
    }
  )) |>
  left_join(
    read_csv(filename2),
    join_by(`Country Code` == Code)
  )

plots <- variables |>
  keep(~ .x %in% names(df) && is.numeric(df[[.x]])) |>
  set_names() |>
  map(
    \(v) {
      x_lab <- attr(df[[v]], "label") %||% v

      x_vals <- df[[v]]
      x_vals_non_na <- x_vals[!is.na(x_vals)]

      # Summary stats
      mean_val <- mean(x_vals_non_na)
      sd_val <- sd(x_vals_non_na)

      nepal_value <- df |>
        filter(`Country Name` == "Nepal") |>
        pull(.data[[v]]) |>
        first()

      # Detect whether values are effectively integers
      is_integerish <- length(x_vals_non_na) > 0 &&
        all(abs(x_vals_non_na - round(x_vals_non_na)) < 1e-8)

      # Choose histogram settings automatically
      if (is_integerish && diff(range(x_vals_non_na)) <= 50) {
        hist_geom <- geom_histogram(
          binwidth = 1,
          boundary = -0.5,
          color = "gray40",
          fill = "gray80",
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      } else {
        # Freedman-Diaconis rule for continuous variables
        iqr_val <- IQR(x_vals_non_na)
        n_val <- length(x_vals_non_na)

        fd_binwidth <- 2 * iqr_val / (n_val^(1 / 3))
        fd_binwidth <- 0.5 * fd_binwidth

        # Fallback if IQR is zero or binwidth is not usable
        if (!is.finite(fd_binwidth) || fd_binwidth <= 0) {
          rng <- diff(range(x_vals_non_na))
          fd_binwidth <- if (is.finite(rng) && rng > 0) rng / 30 else 1
        }

        hist_geom <- geom_histogram(
          binwidth = fd_binwidth,
          color = "gray40",
          fill = "gray80",
          na.rm = TRUE
        )
      }

      caption_text <- paste0(
        "Mean = ",
        scales::number(mean_val, accuracy = 0.01),
        "   |   SD = ",
        scales::number(sd_val, accuracy = 0.01)
      )

      p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = .data[[v]])) +
        hist_geom +
        annotate(
          "rect",
          xmin = mean_val - sd_val,
          xmax = mean_val + sd_val,
          ymin = -Inf,
          ymax = Inf,
          fill = "blue",
          alpha = 0.12
        ) +
        geom_vline(
          xintercept = mean_val,
          color = "blue",
          linewidth = 0.9,
          alpha = 0.48
        ) +
        # geom_vline(
        #   xintercept = c(mean_val - sd_val, mean_val + sd_val),
        #   color = "blue",
        #   linetype = "dashed",
        #   linewidth = 0.8
        # ) +
        labs(
          title = paste("Histogram of", x_lab),
          x = x_lab,
          y = "Count",
          caption = caption_text
        ) +
        theme_minimal() +
        theme(
          plot.caption = element_text(
            hjust = 0.5,
            margin = margin(t = 8)
          ),
          plot.caption.position = "plot"
        )

      if (!is.na(nepal_value)) {
        p <- p +
          geom_vline(
            xintercept = nepal_value,
            color = "red",
            linetype = "dotted",
            linewidth = 0.8
          )
      }
